claims.text: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a primarily FCC matrix.
The as-built alloy has minimal pre-existing oxidation and a fine microstructure.
High-temperature degradation is primarily governed by the evolution and integrity of a mixed Al2O3-TiO2 surface scale.
The ambient gas environment governs formation and integrity of the oxide scale.
Under oxidizing conditions, selective oxidation of Al and Ti produces a mixed oxide scale.
The oxide scale formed under oxidizing conditions is initially protective.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the oxide and metal builds interfacial stress and eventually causes scale separation or spallation.
Scale spallation exposes reactive substrate areas, including Cr-rich regions, that then oxidize rapidly.
A reducing environment hinders protective-scale formation or partially reduces the protective oxides.
A discontinuous or unstable scale under reducing conditions accelerates localized corrosion.
Compromised scale integrity initiates and propagates cracks that can produce catastrophic failure.
Grain-boundary oxidation is an additional structural mediator of degradation.
Prolonged or cyclic oxidizing exposure will produce scale spallation, increased surface roughness, and interfacial cracking.
Reducing exposure will produce patchy oxide coverage and more rapid localized corrosion and embrittlement than the as-built baseline.
The proposed governing behavior applies over 800-1000 °C because oxidation and reduction kinetics are activated in this interval.
Tens to hundreds of hours are sufficient to promote relevant scale evolution.
Identical coupons will be compared under oxidizing and reducing atmospheres at 900 °C for 100, 200, and 300 hours, including thermal cycling.

The hypothesis is falsified if the atmosphere groups show similar scale characteristics and no significant differences in adherence, cracking, or mechanical degradation relative to the as-built baseline.
